psych.headline: Coping and risk are shaped by inner resources and context
points: Risk behaviors cluster: among 2,478 Italian teens, those with both drinking and eating-disorder traits reported the most food-and-alcohol disturbance despite drinking about as much as a drinking-only group (AUDIT 6.21 vs 6.15).

Inner and social resources act as buffers: more mindful adolescents (n = 732) reported less emotional eating, especially girls, and more personal social capital went with fewer depressive symptoms among 1,910 medical students (B = −0.22).

Early experience and framing steer outcomes: in 345 adults, maltreatment linked to stronger stress responses via frustrated competence (β = 0.083), and a warm chatbot reply raised travel intention more than a task-focused one.

edu.headline: AI enters schooling, with humans still in the loop
points: Causal evidence for classroom AI is positive: a pre-registered trial with 7,200 students at 19 universities found instructor-designed AI raised scores on proctored, AI-proof exams.
AI content still needs teacher checks: VeriMath produced verifier-approved math exam drafts for 47 of 50 requirements, but strict teacher review accepted at most 56.8% of items.

Home and peer context shape digital learning: digital parenting predicted more e-learning engagement, most in lower-class families, and AI use for schoolwork went with more school belonging and less loneliness in PISA data from four Chinese regions.

tech.headline: Security shifts to auditing what systems actually do
points: Agent tools must be checked against their code: ACaM found hundreds of structural vulnerabilities across 43 real AI agents, confirming ten with working exploits.

Purpose-built detectors beat general models: a typed decision model topped three LLMs at phishing detection (F1 82.6%) at a fraction of the cost, and FlowSH caught 70% of SQL injections a leading firewall missed without decrypting traffic.
Production and provenance results are concrete: Google's HardwareDx cut GPU-fleet downtime 18.3%, and a reissue-aware watermark told current from superseded images with 99.7% accuracy.

ai.headline: Agents are fast and capable but overconfident where it counts
points: Overconfidence is the key risk: vision-language agents reading emergency CT/MRI were right 30% of the time vs 77% for radiologists, kept their first guess in 63% of runs, and claimed ~90% confidence while being right 38.9% of the time.

Much agent effort is wasted, and cheap fixes help: about 80% of a coding agent's tokens went into calls that did not advance the change, and SpecLook's speculate-then-verify trick made image agents up to 9.9× faster and more accurate.

Oversight and auditability are improving: a trained observer role flagged problem behavior with AUROC 0.907 vs 0.828 for transcript monitoring, and a non-text clinical decision agent matched an LLM agent's 86% diagnostic accuracy in 2.2 s instead of ~95 s.

fin.headline: AI reshapes finance work, but tests need care
points: AI is reorganizing knowledge work: federal civil self-representation rose 6.6 points relative to a comparison group, while top law firms grew revenue 13% on flat billable hours.

New AI signals look promising but need careful testing: retrieving similar past price charts more than doubled a strategy's Sharpe ratio in backtests, while a research benchmark found look-ahead leaks in 50.8% of passing LLM agent runs.

Better models target speed and regime shifts: a spectral method priced corridor products ~60× faster than finite differences, and an adaptive fuzzy-map forecaster beat an LSTM by 7.6 points on return direction.

papers.title: Eating Psychopathology and Alcohol Use in Food and Alcohol Disturbance Among Adolescents: A Person-Centred and Dimensional Analysis
papers.authors: Paolo Meneguzzo, Federico Suprani, Federica Pinna
papers.summary: Among 2,478 Italian teens, those with both drinking and eating-disorder traits reported the most "drunkorexia"-style behavior, even though their alcohol use matched a drinking-only group.
findings: Four profiles: alcohol-risk 33.5%, high psychopathology 27.4%, eating psychopathology 22.0%, low-risk 17.1%.
Alcohol-risk and high-psychopathology groups had nearly the same AUDIT scores (6.15 vs. 6.21), but the latter reported more food-and-alcohol disturbance.
Eating-disorder risk added ΔR² = 0.027 beyond alcohol use, and amplified its effect (interaction ΔR² = 0.022).
papers.takeaway: Alcohol use is the main driver, but screening for eating pathology adds information; caveat: cross-sectional and small added variance.

papers.title: Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration in the Association Between Childhood Maltreatment and Adult Stress Response: A Cross-Sectional Study of Chinese Adults
papers.authors: Yangyang Lei, Haixia Gu, Chunyu Liu
papers.summary: Adults who were maltreated as children reported stronger stress responses partly through feeling less competent: competence frustration was the only indirect path that survived correction (β = 0.083, FDR p = 0.002).
findings: 345 Chinese adults (74 with a psychiatric diagnosis), adjusting for age, sex, socioeconomic status and diagnosis.
Competence and autonomy frustration were linked to higher stress response; competence satisfaction to lower.
No robust evidence that psychiatric diagnosis changed the pattern.
papers.takeaway: Points to competence-building as a possible target for helping maltreatment survivors manage stress; caveat: cross-sectional data cannot show causal mechanisms, as the authors note.

papers.title: Mindfulness and Emotional Eating Among Adolescents: The Mediating Role of Emotion Regulation Flexibility and the Moderating Role of Sex
papers.authors: Yaoyao Zhang, Xin Liu, Wei Gao
papers.summary: More mindful teenagers reported less emotional eating, partly because they were more flexible in how they regulated emotions, and this pathway was stronger in girls.
findings: 732 Chinese adolescents surveyed once.
Emotion regulation inertia and diversity mediated the mindfulness–emotional eating link; sex moderated the diversity path.
The abstract reports no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Suggests mindfulness programs aimed at emotional eating may work through regulation flexibility, especially for girls; caveat: single cross-sectional survey, no effect sizes reported.

papers.title: Personal Social Capital on Depressive Symptoms Among College Students at a Medical University in China: The Moderated Mediating Role of Implicit Health Beliefs and Adverse Childhood Experiences
papers.authors: Xinxin Lai, Jinghong Huang, Xiaojun Liu
papers.summary: Students with more personal social capital reported fewer depressive symptoms (B = −0.22), and about a quarter of that link (25.3%) ran through their implicit beliefs about health.
findings: Survey of 1,910 Chinese medical-university students using PHQ-9 and standard social-capital, health-belief and childhood-adversity scales.
Health beliefs partly mediated the link, accounting for 25.32% of the total effect.
Adverse childhood experiences changed the strength of all three paths (e.g. beliefs → depression B = 0.052, p < 0.05).
papers.takeaway: Points to social ties and health mindsets as joint targets for student mental-health support; cross-sectional data from one university cannot show cause.

papers.title: How Chatbot Advice Shapes Travel Intention: Comparing Social-Oriented and Task-Oriented Responses to Social Media-Induced Travel Anxiety
papers.authors: Zhao Wang, Junzhu Zhang, Jinzhe Yan
papers.summary: A warm, social-style chatbot reply made people more willing to travel than a task-focused one, mainly by easing the travel anxiety that social media had stirred up.
findings: Three scenario experiments: participants imagined browsing travel posts and then read a social- or task-oriented chatbot reply.
Studies 1 and 2: social-oriented replies raised travel intention; in Study 2 reduced anxiety significantly explained that effect.
Study 3: the anxiety pathway was stronger for people with low confidence in their decision. The abstract gives no sample sizes or effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Chatbot tone, not just content, shapes decisions under anxiety; results come from imagined scenarios rather than real bookings.
papers.evidence: Three online experiments · sample sizes not in abstract

papers.title: Digital Parenting and Children's E-Learning Behavior: A Moderated Mediation Analysis in China
papers.authors: Peng Xu, Yu Hou
papers.summary: Children whose parents guided their digital lives more engaged more in online learning, with the biggest benefit in lower-class families.
findings: National survey data (2022 Chinese Minors' Digital Life and Online Protection Survey); held under IV, weighting and double-ML checks.
Effect ran partly through children seeing the internet as useful and through social participation.
The abstract reports no sample size or effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Suggests parental digital guidance can partly offset disadvantage; caveat: observational data.
papers.evidence: Observational survey analysis · national sample (size not stated)

papers.title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
papers.authors: Quy P. Nguyen, Duong Q. Nguyen, Dinh P. T. Nguyen
papers.summary: An AI pipeline produced verifier-approved math exam drafts for 47 of 50 curriculum requirements, but strict teacher review accepted at most 56.8% of items.
findings: Built on 4,555 Vietnamese Grade 12 math items, tested on 50 generation requirements with two model backbones.
Verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run.
Up to 56.8% of generated items passed strict teacher-readiness checks.
papers.takeaway: AI can speed up exam writing, but teachers still need to review roughly half of items; caveat: one national curriculum.

papers.title: Socioeconomic Status and AI Use for Schoolwork in Relation to Adolescents' School Belonging and Loneliness in Four Chinese Regions
papers.authors: Jie Xu, Kai Gao, Jiefei Luo
papers.summary: Teens who used AI more for schoolwork, and those from better-off families, felt more belonging and less loneliness at school.
findings: PISA data from four Chinese regions, regressions with school fixed effects and false-discovery correction.
Higher family status and more AI use for schoolwork both linked to lower loneliness and greater belonging.
Peer help-seeking only modestly buffered the status–loneliness link; family support did not; no sample size or effect sizes in the abstract.
papers.takeaway: Pushes back on fears that AI homework help isolates students; caveat: cross-sectional associations only.

papers.title: General Teaching Self-Efficacy, Innovative Work Behavior, and Perceived Interdisciplinary Teaching Capacity Among Chinese Physical Education Teachers: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Miao Miao, Luying Jiao, Shuhong Wang
papers.summary: PE teachers' readiness to teach across subjects tracked their habit of innovating (β = 0.665), not their general teaching confidence (β = 0.043, not significant).
findings: 668 usable responses from PE teachers in 8 Chinese regions (714 collected).
Innovative work behavior β = 0.665, p < 0.001; general self-efficacy β = 0.043, p = 0.195.
Difference between the two Δβ = 0.622 (95% CI 0.509–0.735).
papers.takeaway: Suggests training should build innovation practices like joint planning, not just confidence; caveat: self-reports with overlapping item formats.

papers.title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
papers.authors: Jun Li, Robert Bray, Sébastien Martin
papers.summary: In a pre-registered randomized trial with 7,200 students at 19 universities, AI tools designed by the course instructors improved learning on proctored, in-person exams that students could not use AI on.
findings: Ran over three semesters; learning was measured with AI-proof, proctored assessments.
Student engagement (course activity) and satisfaction (course evaluations) did not change.
The abstract does not report effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Rare large-scale causal evidence that course-specific AI can raise real learning, not just homework scores; caveat: size of the gain is not given in the abstract.

papers.title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
papers.authors: Monika Santra, Dhilung Kirat, Qiushi Wu
papers.summary: Reading an AI agent's tool source code, rather than trusting tool descriptions, exposed hundreds of structural vulnerabilities across 43 real agents, ten confirmed with working exploits.
findings: Recovered tool capabilities with 98.3% macro-F1 on 24 hand-annotated agents.
Reconstructed injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the best baseline.
Across 43 real-world agents (9 multi-agent), found hundreds of vulnerabilities; 10 confirmed with proof-of-concept exploits.
papers.takeaway: Gives agent builders a way to audit what tools can actually do, not what they claim; caveat: severity of the unconfirmed findings is unclear.

papers.title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
papers.authors: Muhammad Mahir Malik, Muhammad Moiz Khalid, Hussain Ahmad
papers.summary: A small typed decision model beat three large LLMs at flagging phishing emails (F1 82.6%) while being faster, cheaper and better calibrated.
findings: 1,500 labeled emails; Jev 1.13 had the best accuracy (79.7%), recall (98.0%) and F1 (82.6%), though precision was 71.4%.
Lowest batch time (174 s), token use and cost (about $0.015 per 1,000 decisions) among the four systems.
Best calibration too (Brier 0.170, ECE 0.159).
papers.takeaway: Suggests purpose-built models can outdo general LLMs for security triage; caveat: high false-positive rate and LLM explanations were not evaluated.

papers.title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs
papers.authors: Nuno Durão, Rodrigo Branco, Vinicius V. Cogo
papers.summary: Combining flow metadata with server logs caught 70% of the SQL injection attacks that a leading web application firewall missed, without decrypting traffic.
findings: Works on HTTP and HTTPS with no in-transit decryption.
Unsupervised anomaly detection on NetFlow plus similarity search over server logs.
Detected 70% of SQL injections that ModSecurity missed in a testbed with multiple web scanners.
papers.takeaway: A privacy-friendlier complement to firewalls; caveat: lab testbed with scanner traffic, not live attacks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · testbed with multiple web scanners

papers.title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
papers.authors: Xinyuan Li, Yi Nian, Xiaoqin Feng
papers.summary: A watermark that tracks an image's edit history told current from superseded versions with 99.7% accuracy and pinpointed the latest approved edit region after three reissues.
findings: 480 editing histories across four releases, including AI editors' outputs.
99.67% accuracy on current vs. superseded; 94.09% recall on unissued edits.
After three reissues: 93.13% median region-label accuracy and 92.86% IoU for the latest approved revision.
papers.takeaway: Moves provenance beyond "is this real" to "is this the current approved version"; caveat: tested on a constructed set of edit histories.

papers.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
papers.authors: Yuanlin Wen, Elan Markowitz, Zubo Gu
papers.summary: A graph foundation model deployed in Google datacenters cut production downtime for GPU machines by 18.3% and for TPU machines by 16.1%.
findings: Used in production for hardware diagnosis and repair.
Downtime down 18.3% (GPU) and 16.1% (TPU).
Quality-assurance time down 28.3% (GPU) and 25.1% (TPU).
papers.takeaway: Rare production evidence that ML-driven diagnosis saves real fleet time; caveat: one company's fleet, details of the comparison baseline not in the abstract.

papers.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
papers.authors: Alex Lin Wang, Linus Yifeng Tang, Dami Choi
papers.summary: A separate "observer" role trained only to answer questions about the assistant's own behavior caught problems best, with a mean AUROC of 0.907 across five held-out oversight tests.
findings: Observer built on Qwen3.6-27B: mean AUROC 0.907 on five held-out oversight evaluations.
Baselines scored lower: honesty training 0.864, transcript monitoring 0.828, activation oracles 0.796.
The other oversight methods also did better on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant.
papers.takeaway: Points to a cheap, trainable way for models to report on their own behavior for safety audits; caveat: tested on one model family and a handful of evaluations.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
papers.authors: Jonathan Lichtle, Aymen Meddeb, Antonin Birot
papers.summary: AI agents that scrolled through emergency CT and MRI scans on their own got the diagnosis right only 30% of the time on cases where radiologists scored 77%, while claiming about 90% confidence.
findings: 6 vision-language models, 100 exams, 4 conditions, 4,800 runs; pooled accuracy 32.6% with free navigation vs. 42–43% when handed all or key slices.
Models stuck with their first guess in 63.1% of runs; after a wrong first guess they ended correct only 12.4% of the time.
Median stated confidence 90%, but only 38.9% of answers were correct.
papers.takeaway: A strong warning against letting current AI agents read imaging unsupervised: they anchor early and are badly overconfident; caveat: 100 exams from one setting.
papers.evidence: Preprint · 4,800 model runs on 100 exams, vs. radiologists on 30 cases

papers.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
papers.authors: Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Varinia Bernales
papers.summary: About 80% of the tokens a coding agent spends in a successful run go into calls that leave the code change no closer to done.
findings: In repeated code/uncode cycles, ~80% of tokens in successful runs were "heat" that did not move the requested change.
The estimated minimum cost of a change was 14–22% of the mean cost of a successful run.
Making a change cost 1.1–1.5× as much as undoing it.
papers.takeaway: Suggests large efficiency headroom for coding agents and a new way to measure it; caveat: a physics-inspired framing tested on controlled cycles, not real projects.

papers.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
papers.authors: Tiancheng Bao, Riga Wu, Jan Wienhold
papers.summary: A non-text decision agent matched an LLM agent's diagnostic accuracy on emergency admissions (86.5% vs. 86.1%) while working up each patient in about 2 seconds instead of ~95.
findings: 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases: 86.5% diagnostic accuracy vs. 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent.
Median work-up time 2.2 s vs. 92–100 s; its most confident diagnoses were correct 98.5% of the time.
Beat the best of three 24-hour severity scores in 5 of 8 ICU cohorts using only 2–6 hours of records.
papers.takeaway: Shows auditable, action-level clinical agents can match LLM agents far faster; caveat: retrospective records, not prospective use.
papers.evidence: Preprint · retrospective evaluation on 546 admissions + 8 ICU cohorts

papers.title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
papers.authors: Xi Ding, Jiawei Zhang
papers.summary: Letting a small model guess where to zoom, and skipping the expensive tool loop when it is confident, made image-reasoning agents up to 9.9× faster while also more accurate.
findings: Beat every baseline on every split of V*, HR-Bench and POPE, with 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy.
7.7× and 4.7× speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents; the Fast variant reached 9.9× and 6.3×.
Needs no training.
papers.takeaway: A cheap speculate-then-verify trick that cuts the cost of "thinking with images" agents; caveat: benchmark results only.

papers.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
papers.authors: Liu Zhang, Mark Esposito, Isabel Yang
papers.summary: Self-representation in U.S. federal civil cases rose 6.6 percentage points relative to a comparison group by 2025, while the biggest law firms grew revenue 13% on nearly flat billable hours.
findings: Difference-in-differences across 89 federal districts: non-prisoner self-representation up 6.6 pp vs. prisoner petitions by FY2025.
No clear post-2022 shift of lawyer employment into client firms; lower-priced firms saw stronger demand growth.
Much of the reallocation started before generative AI.
papers.takeaway: Early sign that AI is changing who buys and who does legal work; caveat: timing makes AI attribution uncertain.

papers.title: When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction
papers.authors: Hui Chen, Haoyu Liu, Ke Wu
papers.summary: Finding the most similar-looking past price charts with an image model predicted stock returns, and tuning the model to returns more than doubled the strategy's Sharpe ratio.
findings: Three decades of U.S. stock price data.
An off-the-shelf image representation already picked neighbors whose returns predicted the cross-section; return-aligned tuning more than doubled the Sharpe ratio and beat a CNN trained on charts.
Predictability was concentrated in harder-to-arbitrage stocks; the abstract gives no exact Sharpe values.
papers.takeaway: Suggests chart patterns carry exploitable information, mainly where arbitrage is costly; caveat: backtest only.
papers.evidence: Preprint · backtest on 30 years of U.S. stocks

papers.title: Spectral Pricing of Corridor Products under Layered Local Volatility
papers.authors: Andrey Itkin, Dmitry Muravey
papers.summary: A spectral method priced barrier corridor products about 60× faster than a standard finite-difference approach, with accuracy near rounding error.
findings: Agreed with independent calculations to near rounding error.
Kept full accuracy at volatility layer boundaries, where tested finite-difference grids lost an order of convergence.
~60× faster for the accrual distribution than the tested finite-difference scheme.
papers.takeaway: Faster, more accurate pricing for a common exotic derivative; caveat: numerical benchmarks, not market data.

papers.title: BuySideFlow: A Point-in-Time Benchmark for LLM Agents in Investment Research
papers.authors: Dong Bo, Fanjin Zhang, Ke Cheng
papers.summary: LLM agents doing investment research got only 16.2% to 36.8% of answers right, and half of the 'passing' runs used information that would not have been available at the time.
findings: Nine agent configurations over 408 tasks.
Result accuracy ranged from 16.2% to 36.8%.
Look-ahead (point-in-time) violations appeared in 193 of 380 passing runs (50.8%).
papers.takeaway: Backtests of AI investment agents may be inflated by look-ahead leakage; this is one benchmark's task set.

papers.title: Online-Adaptive Fuzzy Cognitive Maps for Neuro-symbolic Financial Forecasting
papers.authors: Brandon Rodriguez, Abel Deulofeu, Olaoluwa Adigun
papers.summary: An interpretable, self-updating forecasting model beat an LSTM by 7.6 percentage points at predicting whether returns go up or down, and re-adjusted to new market regimes within 10–15 trading days.
findings: Framework I beat an LSTM by 7.6 points on return-sign accuracy.
Framework II scored 68.9% to 85.7% on state-direction accuracy.
Adaptive maps converged to new regimes in 10–15 trading days.
papers.takeaway: Offers an explainable alternative to black-box forecasters; accuracy gains are not tested as trading profits after costs.
